book_context: These are the four closing chapters of an autobiography told in the third person. Its leitmotif is a failed 'education.' Recurring threads in this stretch: the steps of Ara Coeli in Rome, where Adams sits to puzzle over history's failures; Russia as 'inertia'; the Virgin set against the Dynamo as rival forces; Unity against Multiplicity; the 'conservative Christian anarchist' joke; Karl Pearson's 'Grammar of Science'; the coal-output as a measure of progress; and the three friends Adams, Hay and King. Chapter XXXII moves from the eve of the Russo-Japanese War through the St. Louis Exposition and a summer of Virgin-pilgrimage to the decision to write a theory. Chapter XXXIII states that theory. Chapter XXXIV adds a law of acceleration. Chapter XXXV returns to New York, Roosevelt and the Trusts, Hay's decline and death, and ends in silence. Several earlier chapters are omitted from the abridgment, so local allusions to them (the Markoe house, the caravan image, Bacon via Langley) must stay self-explaining.
continuity_checks: The Edict of Milan is 313, the Milvian Bridge the year before, the sack of Rome 410, and Hippo around 430.
The Augustine quotation must be attributed to Augustine, not to Adams.
Keep the hedges ('for convenience,' 'rather recklessly') so speculation is not presented as fact.
The final paragraph must point forward to an acceleration formula without stating it.

essential: Definitions: progress, force, and man as a force; the theory admits it begs the question.
The inversion that forces capture man; the spider-in-web image with its fatal mistakes; man's early teachers (fire, water, animals, grains).
Man worships the whole as unity and God, even while blundering in choosing particular forces; religion as cultivation of occult force; hunger for infinite power as motive.
Antiquity progressed by economies, not new force (mathematics, Civil Law, coinage, roads); the means of motion stayed old.

The scandal of Rome's fall around 305 at the height of success, where Adams broke down on the steps of Ara Coeli. He rejects mineral exhaustion and argues the empire generated too much energy, too fast.

Unity on earth forced unity in heaven: Constantine's 'trust' (keep the Edict quotation as an 'Act of Congress'); In hoc signo vinces; Theodosius against Eugene as a boxing-match; the Cross as fetish-power like X-rays.
Slave and fetish as Rome's only engines; the vicious circle; Alaric in 410; Augustine's defence of spiritual over mechanical value, with his quotation.
The Middle Ages as a long experiment on occult force, producing architecture and art; Byzantium shows more varied forces.
The sudden arrival of the compass (which educated) and of Greek fire and gunpowder (diabolic educators), with St. Louis kneeling at Greek fire.

Even the innovators thought they served the Cross (Gutenberg, Columbus, Luther, the Puritans; the Church condemning anarchists, not atheists). Scientists doubted only the personality of Unity, never Unity itself.

Bacon reverses thought and force (keep at least one Bacon maxim). Acceleration after 1500 is involuntary; resistance is constant; a few score conductors like Franklin; then Newton, Franklin and Watt as men to whom forces 'stuck.'

New force is not in itself good; supersensual forces in 1900; the formula is admitted to be the oldest theory, with religion, philosophy and science diverging only at the edge (chaos or unity). It is a chart of convenience and needs a formula of acceleration.

title: A DYNAMIC THEORY OF HISTORY (1904)

verbatim.purpose: Self-undercutting definition that founds the theory.
verbatim.text: A DYNAMIC theory, like most theories, begins by begging the question: it defines Progress as the development and economy of Forces.
The sum of force attracts; the feeble atom or molecule called man is attracted; he suffers education or growth; he is the sum of the forces that attract him;

verbatim.purpose: Aphoristic triad, the theory's ethic of education.
verbatim.text: Susceptibility to the highest forces is the highest genius; selection between them is the highest science; their mass is the highest educator.

verbatim.purpose: Signature comic-commercial reading of the Edict of Milan.
verbatim.text: Good taste forbids saying that Constantine the Great speculated as audaciously as a modern stock-broker on values of which he knew at the utmost only the volume;

verbatim.purpose: Concrete deflation of religion as fetish-power.
verbatim.text: The laity, the people, the million, almost to a man, bet on the gods as they bet on a horse.

verbatim.purpose: Thesis linking the medieval and modern sections.
verbatim.text: This persistence of thought-inertia is the leading idea of modern history.

verbatim.purpose: The Baconian reversal stated as law.
verbatim.text: thought did not evolve nature, but nature evolved thought.

verbatim.purpose: Analogy that ties 1900 to the year 300; it closes the historical sweep.
verbatim.text: before which the man of science stood at first as bewildered and helpless as, in the fourth century, a priest of Isis before the Cross of Christ.

voice_profile: Late Adams writes as an aged, ironic observer who calls himself 'Adams,' 'the student,' 'the historian,' 'the pilgrim,' or 'a historical tramp.' The voice moves between social observation and cosmic analogy. Political events, cathedrals and expositions are read as measures of force. The core devices are: self-deprecating claims of ignorance set against sweeping generalization; borrowed scientific vocabulary (inertia, mass, acceleration, perihelion, the formula s = gt^2/2) applied to history; long periodic sentences built from semicolons and double-hyphen asides; paradox and reversal ('the more he was educated, the less he understood'); and mock-commercial metaphor ('Trust of State Religions'). He hedges constantly ('for convenience,' 'one might assume') while sounding prophetic. The ending turns from argument to elegy for John Hay and Clarence King, closing on silence and quiet irony.
